For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
The paper proposes raising three main-course prices and removing the mushroom risotto from 1 April. It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%.

I checked it against Table 1 and §§2 and 4. **The price arithmetic is correct, but the case for removing the risotto is contradicted by the table: it has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest. The projection also ignores the beef cost rise in §4, which falls on two of the three dishes being repriced.**

## 1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest

From Table 1: (£14.00 − £2.80) / £14.00 = **80%**, the highest of any main. The weakest margin belongs to the sirloin steak at 60%, which the paper proposes to *raise* the price of. On sales, risotto's 90 plates a week ties with the specials for lowest, so "lowest sales" is true but shared.

Replacing an 80%-margin dish with a special risks *lowering* overall margin. Specials currently run at 64%. A special at £14.00 with that margin would earn about £2.24 less per plate, roughly **£200 a week less** across 90 plates.

Low sales could still be a good reason to rethink the dish. If so, that should be the stated argument, and the replacement special should be costed to match or beat 80%.

## 2. The beef increase isn't in the projection

§4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April. The same date applies to the burger and steak prices. If all of each plate's food cost were beef, the extra cost would be:

| Dish | Current food cost | After +12% | Extra per plate | Weekly (plates) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | £0.50 | £131 (260) |
| Steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | £1.25 | £150 (120) |

That is **up to about £280 a week**. It's an upper bound, since not every pound of plate cost is beef. Even so, a large part of the burger and steak price rises would only cover the beef increase rather than restore margin. The extra gross profit is probably **£530–£810 a week**, not £810.

## 3. Check whether the figures include VAT

UK menu prices include 20% VAT, but Table 1 appears to work out margins on those VAT-inclusive prices. If so, each £1.00 price rise adds only about £0.83 of net revenue. The £810 becomes about **£675 a week (£35,100 a year)** before the beef cost, and every margin in the table is overstated. Fish and chips, for example, is about 63% on its net price of £13.75, not 69%.

Your accountant or till reports will show which basis the "70% target" uses. Whichever it is, the paper should be consistent.

## 4. The 71% margin

Using Table 1, and assuming specials sell at about £15, the current main-course margin is around **69.4%**. Adding £810 of revenue takes it to about **70.8%**, so "about 71%" is right *before* the beef rise and any VAT adjustment. Including the beef rise, it is about **69.2%**, slightly *below* today's level. The increases mostly offset rising costs rather than restore margin.

## 5. How much volume can fall before the gain disappears

The paper assumes volumes hold because guests are loyal. A 60% repeat rate shows loyalty, but regulars are also the guests most likely to notice a price change. The useful figure is the break-even point.

Fish and chips gross profit per plate goes from £11.40 to £12.40, so sales can fall about **8%** before the price rise loses money on that dish. The burger and steak are similar. That gives a concrete monitoring threshold.

**The monitoring baseline needs fixing.** January–February is typically a quiet period, so spring trade will look higher regardless of prices. Compare the same weeks last year instead, or track each dish's share of total mains.

## 6. Smaller corrections

- **Trading days:** §2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. §8 says "six trading days." Fix §8. The weekly figures don't depend on it, but the annual total assumes 52 trading weeks, so allow for closure periods.
- **"Value option":** All three new prices are below the competitor midpoint (fish £17.50 against £17.98; burger £16.00 against £16.50; steak £28.00 against £29.50). But none would still be the cheapest in the area. Each moves above the lowest competitor price (£16.95, £15.50, £27.00). "Below the local midpoint" is accurate; "the value option" overstates it.
- **Weekday lunch:** §7 calls it a small share, but only Friday and Saturday dinners are quantified. A figure for lunch would back this up.

## 7. What holds up

- The Table 1 margins are correctly calculated from the stated prices and costs, apart from the VAT question.
- The weekly figure is right: £310 + £260 + £240 = £810, which is £42,120 over 52 weeks.
- Each proposed price sits below the competitor midpoint.
- Raising prices is a reasonable response to an overall margin that has slipped from 70% to 67% with no change since September 2024.

## Recommendation for the paper

1. Reverse the reasoning on the risotto. Keep it, or replace it with a special costed to at least 80%.
2. Net off the beef increase in §5.3, and clarify the VAT basis.
3. Present the extra gross profit as a range, roughly £530–£810 a week before VAT adjustment.
4. Add an 8% volume-drop trigger, measured against the same weeks last year.

On those corrections, the price increases still look sensible. They mainly protect margin against rising costs rather than lift it to 71%.
